verdict:
NULL, but SUPERSEDING script 66, whose null was not valid. That run cut both populations at one fixed 0.530 mag -- 5.35 sigma for the reference against 1.81 sigma for the pristine high-RUWE sample -- and compared residuals built by two different estimators (a degree-5 refit at sigma 0.1767 against the pipeline local-slope column at 0.0991). Both errors widen the high-RUWE distribution relative to the reference and so suppress its apparent one-sidedness; its headline 3.96-against-22.60 comparison is meaningless and must not be cited.

Corrected -- one polynomial, one box, one distance support, counted at k sigma of each population's own scatter -- the pristine high-RUWE sample is 1.68x the reference ratio at k=2 (4.51 against 2.68, p = 6.3e-60) but 0.76x at k=3 (4.56 against 6.04). The excess SHRINKS as the cut moves out. An added population of dim objects would do the reverse, becoming more conspicuous the harder it is isolated, so the 2-sigma excess is extra symmetric scatter -- expected, since high-RUWE stars have genuinely degraded astrometry and hence noisier distance moduli -- and not a one-sided dim tail.

The pristine cut is doing its job, which is the other thing script 66 could not demonstrate: the blended subsample runs at 10.88 (k=2) and 22.67 (k=3), against 4.51 and 4.56 pristine. That is the known one-signed contaminant -- 2MASS aperture mismatch in a 4 arcsec beam brightens Ks and so manufactures a dim residual -- being suppressed by roughly a factor of 5 at k=3. Because that contaminant is one-signed, the bright tail is a conservative mirror rather than a clean false-positive rate, so no numerical limit on f is quoted from this channel.
